poem.title: Ode to a Nightingale
poem.author: John Keats
poem.text:
My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains
My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,
Or emptied some dull opiate to the drains
One minute past, and Lethe-wards had sunk:
'Tis not through envy of thy happy lot,
But being too happy in thine happiness,—
That thou, light-winged Dryad of the trees,
In some melodious plot
Of beechen green, and shadows numberless,
Singest of summer in full-throated ease.

O, for a draught of vintage! that hath been
Cool'd a long age in the deep-delved earth,
Tasting of Flora and the country green,
Dance, and Provençal song, and sunburnt mirth!
O for a beaker full of the warm South,
Full of the true, the blushful Hippocrene,
With beaded bubbles winking at the brim,
And purple-stained mouth;
That I might drink, and leave the world unseen,
And with thee fade away into the forest dim:

Fade far away, dissolve, and quite forget
What thou among the leaves hast never known,
The weariness, the fever, and the fret
Here, where men sit and hear each other groan;
Where palsy shakes a few, sad, last gray hairs,
Where youth grows pale, and spectre-thin, and dies;
Where but to think is to be full of sorrow
And leaden-eyed despairs,
Where Beauty cannot keep her lustrous eyes,
Or new Love pine at them beyond to-morrow.

Away! away! for I will fly to thee,
Not charioted by Bacchus and his pards,
But on the viewless wings of Poesy,
Though the dull brain perplexes and retards:
Already with thee! tender is the night,
And haply the Queen-Moon is on her throne,
Cluster'd around by all her starry Fays;
But here there is no light,
Save what from heaven is with the breezes blown
Through verdurous glooms and winding mossy ways.

I cannot see what flowers are at my feet,
Nor what soft incense hangs upon the boughs,
But, in embalmed darkness, guess each sweet
Wherewith the seasonable month endows
The grass, the thicket, and the fruit-tree wild;
White hawthorn, and the pastoral eglantine;
Fast fading violets cover'd up in leaves;
And mid-May's eldest child,
The coming musk-rose, full of dewy wine,
The murmurous haunt of flies on summer eves.

Darkling I listen; and, for many a time
I have been half in love with easeful Death,
Call'd him soft names in many a mused rhyme,
To take into the air my quiet breath;
Now more than ever seems it rich to die,
To cease upon the midnight with no pain,
While thou art pouring forth thy soul abroad
In such an ecstasy!
Still wouldst thou sing, and I have ears in vain—
To thy high requiem become a sod.

Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!
No hungry generations tread thee down;
The voice I hear this passing night was heard
In ancient days by emperor and clown:
Perhaps the self-same song that found a path
Through the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home,
She stood in tears amid the alien corn;
The same that oft-times hath
Charm'd magic casements, opening on the foam
Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn.

Forlorn! the very word is like a bell
To toll me back from thee to my sole self!
Adieu! the fancy cannot cheat so well
As she is fam'd to do, deceiving elf.
Adieu! adieu! thy plaintive anthem fades
Past the near meadows, over the still stream,
Up the hill-side; and now 'tis buried deep
In the next valley-glades:
Was it a vision, or a waking dream?
Fled is that music:—Do I wake or sleep?

pages.title: The Whole Song in View
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Keats wrote "Ode to a Nightingale" in 1819, during the extraordinary spring and summer when several of his great odes arrived close together. You will learn this one over sixteen days, in five-line movements. That pace lets the poem keep its luxuriance without becoming a blur.

Today begins before the bird has fully entered the poem. The first five lines are all human heaviness: ache, numbness, poison, opiate, forgetfulness. The nightingale is present as joy, but the speaker reaches it through pain.

pages.title: A Young Poet Near the Edge
pages.bodyMarkdown:
In 1819 Keats was twenty-three. His brother Tom had died of tuberculosis the previous December, and Keats had nursed him closely enough to know what the illness looked like. He had trained in medicine before choosing poetry, so death was not an abstract literary decoration for him. He knew the body from the inside of a ward.

The famous story says he heard a nightingale near Charles Brown's house in Hampstead and wrote under a plum tree. Whether every detail of that memory is tidy matters less than the scene it preserves: a young man, ill and grieving, listening to a bird that seems untouched by the conditions of human life.

pages.title: Pain That Feels Like Sleep
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The first surprise is that joy hurts. "My heart aches" is plain enough, but "drowsy numbness pains" is stranger. Numbness should dull pain. Keats makes it painful in itself, as if the speaker is losing contact with the world and suffering that loss as it happens.

Hemlock, opiate, and Lethe all pull in the same direction. Poison, drug, forgetful river. The speaker is not excited by the bird. He is drugged by it, lowered into a half-death before he can explain why.

pages.title: Hemlock and Lethe
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Keats reaches for classical images almost immediately. Hemlock recalls the poison that killed Socrates. Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the underworld. The opening therefore places the speaker near death, sleep, and oblivion before the poem has even reached the bird's body.

That is one reason the poem feels so unstable. It is not simply about loving nature. It begins with the cost of being human in the presence of something that seems effortlessly alive.

pages.title: Not Envy
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"'Tis not through envy" is a correction before an accusation has been made. The speaker knows how his ache might look. A happier creature is singing nearby, and he is suffering. Envy would be the easy explanation.

He refuses that. The pain comes from being "too happy" in the bird's happiness. That sounds generous, but it is also dangerous. To be too absorbed in another being's joy is to feel your own limits more sharply.

pages.title: A Dryad in the Trees
pages.bodyMarkdown:
A Dryad is a tree nymph. Keats does not say the nightingale is like a Dryad in any careful, cautious way. He lets the myth enter directly. The bird becomes a spirit of the trees, part of the living wood rather than a visitor passing through it.

That tells you something about Keats's imagination. It does not leave nature alone as plain scenery. The grove becomes ancient, peopled, charged with presences. The bird's song opens a mythic space around itself.

pages.title: Ease After Numbness
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"Light-winged" matters because the poem has just given the speaker heaviness. His heart aches. His senses are dull. The bird, by contrast, seems weightless, made for movement, song, and concealment among leaves.

"Full-throated ease" is one of those Keats phrases that feels physically complete. The throat is full, but not strained. Ease here is not laziness. It is unhindered expression, the sound of a life not divided against itself.

pages.title: Heard More Than Seen
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The nightingale is mostly a voice. Keats gives us trees, a plot, green, shadows, and summer, but almost no visual detail of the bird itself. That will matter later, when the speaker enters a darkness where he cannot see the flowers at his feet.

The poem's world is built around hearing. The bird's song creates a place, and the speaker tries to follow it. You can think of the poem as a series of attempted crossings from human consciousness into song.

pages.title: Beechen Green
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"In some melodious plot" is beautifully uncertain. "Some" keeps the exact place hidden. "Plot" can mean a patch of ground, but it also faintly suggests design, as if the song has made a small arranged world inside the trees.

"Beechen green" gives the line a soft, leafy density. "Shadows numberless" expands the place beyond counting. The bird is local, but the imaginative space around it keeps widening.

pages.title: Bacchus at the Door
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The second stanza begins with desire: "O, for a draught." Keats is not yet asking for poetry. He is asking for vintage, for a physical means of transport. The imagined wine has been cooled underground, as if it has absorbed time from the earth itself.

Romantic poets often treat intoxication as a threshold. It loosens the boundaries of ordinary selfhood. Keats is drawn to that possibility, but he will not let it remain simple for long.

pages.title: A Drink with a Landscape Inside
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The wine "tastes" of things it cannot literally contain: Flora, country green, dance, song, mirth. Keats turns taste into a gathering sense. One sip would carry flowers, fields, music, bodies, and sunlight together.

"Deep-delved earth" is especially rich. The doubled d sounds slow the phrase down, and "delved" makes the ground feel worked and ancient. The speaker wants escape, but the fantasy begins by going downward into earth.

pages.title: Old South, Old Music
pages.bodyMarkdown:

The "warm South" is not only geography. It is a climate of imagination: ripe, musical, sensuous, far from the damp English night where the speaker sits listening.

pages.title: The Whole Poem
pages.bodyMarkdown:
My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains
My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,
Or emptied some dull opiate to the drains
One minute past, and Lethe-wards had sunk:
'Tis not through envy of thy happy lot,
But being too happy in thine happiness,—
That thou, light-winged Dryad of the trees,
In some melodious plot
Of beechen green, and shadows numberless,
Singest of summer in full-throated ease.

O, for a draught of vintage! that hath been
Cool'd a long age in the deep-delved earth,
Tasting of Flora and the country green,
Dance, and Provençal song, and sunburnt mirth!
O for a beaker full of the warm South,
Full of the true, the blushful Hippocrene,
With beaded bubbles winking at the brim,
And purple-stained mouth;
That I might drink, and leave the world unseen,
And with thee fade away into the forest dim:

Fade far away, dissolve, and quite forget
What thou among the leaves hast never known,
The weariness, the fever, and the fret
Here, where men sit and hear each other groan;
Where palsy shakes a few, sad, last gray hairs,
Where youth grows pale, and spectre-thin, and dies;
Where but to think is to be full of sorrow
And leaden-eyed despairs,
Where Beauty cannot keep her lustrous eyes,
Or new Love pine at them beyond to-morrow.

Away! away! for I will fly to thee,
Not charioted by Bacchus and his pards,
But on the viewless wings of Poesy,
Though the dull brain perplexes and retards:
Already with thee! tender is the night,
And haply the Queen-Moon is on her throne,
Cluster'd around by all her starry Fays;
But here there is no light,
Save what from heaven is with the breezes blown
Through verdurous glooms and winding mossy ways.

I cannot see what flowers are at my feet,
Nor what soft incense hangs upon the boughs,
But, in embalmed darkness, guess each sweet
Wherewith the seasonable month endows
The grass, the thicket, and the fruit-tree wild;
White hawthorn, and the pastoral eglantine;
Fast fading violets cover'd up in leaves;
And mid-May's eldest child,
The coming musk-rose, full of dewy wine,
The murmurous haunt of flies on summer eves.

Darkling I listen; and, for many a time
I have been half in love with easeful Death,
Call'd him soft names in many a mused rhyme,
To take into the air my quiet breath;
Now more than ever seems it rich to die,
To cease upon the midnight with no pain,
While thou art pouring forth thy soul abroad
In such an ecstasy!
Still wouldst thou sing, and I have ears in vain—
To thy high requiem become a sod.

Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!
No hungry generations tread thee down;
The voice I hear this passing night was heard
In ancient days by emperor and clown:
Perhaps the self-same song that found a path
Through the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home,
She stood in tears amid the alien corn;
The same that oft-times hath
Charm'd magic casements, opening on the foam
Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn.

Forlorn! the very word is like a bell
To toll me back from thee to my sole self!
Adieu! the fancy cannot cheat so well
As she is fam'd to do, deceiving elf.
Adieu! adieu! thy plaintive anthem fades
Past the near meadows, over the still stream,
Up the hill-side; and now 'tis buried deep
In the next valley-glades:
Was it a vision, or a waking dream?
Fled is that music:—Do I wake or sleep?

pages.title: Hippocrene
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Hippocrene was the spring sacred to the Muses. In myth, it was linked with poetic inspiration. By asking for the "blushful Hippocrene," Keats quietly shifts the drink from ordinary wine toward the source of poetry itself.

That prepares the next stanza, where he will reject Bacchus and choose Poesy. For now, wine and poetry are still mingled in one bright cup.

pages.title: Bubbles at the Brim
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"Beaded bubbles winking at the brim" is almost too sensuous to paraphrase, which is usually a sign that Keats is doing exactly what prose cannot do. The bubbles are tactile, visual, and flirtatiously alive.

"Purple-stained mouth" keeps the body in the image. The drink is not an idea. It touches lips, stains them, and leaves evidence. Even the wish to escape begins in sensation.

pages.title: Unseen

Keats's escape is not a clean ascent. It is a fading into the forest, into dimness. The desired release has the colour of disappearance.

pages.title: With Thee
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"With thee" is the emotional hinge. The speaker does not want intoxication for its own sake. He wants to follow the nightingale into the space its song seems to open.

"Fade away" is gentler than "die," but the poem will soon test how far apart those two desires really are. The forest dim is refuge, but it is also a place where outlines disappear.

pages.title: The Sickroom Enters
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Keats had lived close to illness. His mother died when he was young, his brother Tom died in 1818, and Keats himself would soon show unmistakable signs of tuberculosis. Lines like these do not need biography to work, but biography explains why they do not feel decorative.

"Where men sit and hear each other groan" is almost brutally communal. Human beings are not only mortal. They have to listen to one another suffering.

pages.title: Three Nouns in a Row

pages.title: What the Leaves Do Not Know
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The nightingale has "never known" this suffering. Keats is not saying birds are literally immortal or untouched by harm. He is writing from the speaker's perception. The song seems to come from a life beyond human self-awareness.

That distinction matters. The poem is not a scientific claim about a bird. It is a record of what the bird's song makes possible in the listening mind.

pages.title: A Sudden Descent
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"Here" is one of the plainest words in the stanza, and one of the bleakest. After vintage, Flora, Hippocrene, and the forest dim, the poem lands in a room where men hear each other groan.

"Palsy" makes suffering old and visible. The shaking hairs are "few," "sad," and "last." Keats slows the line down with adjectives, as if the body itself has become something painfully countable.

pages.title: Against Easy Consolation
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Keats is often remembered as a poet of beauty, which is true but incomplete. He is also a poet of beauty under threat. He does not treat beautiful things as a cure for mortality. More often, beauty hurts because it is radiant and passing.

That tension is central here. Beauty has "lustrous eyes," but it cannot keep them. The line refuses to let loveliness become a shelter from time.

pages.title: Youth as Ghost

pages.title: Beauty and Love as Figures

The phrase "beyond to-morrow" is deliberately small. Against the grandeur of Beauty and Love, tomorrow is painfully near.

pages.title: The Repeated Where
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The repeated "Where" binds the stanza together. It makes human life feel like a single place with several rooms: age, sickness, youth, thought, beauty, love. Everywhere the speaker looks, time has already entered.

The nightingale matters more because of this. Its song seems to come from outside the "Where" of human life, or at least from a place where human sorrow has no authority.

pages.title: The God Left Behind
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Bacchus is the god of wine, ecstasy, and revelry. His "pards" are leopards, the animals traditionally linked with his chariot. Keats gives the rejected option a splendid image before refusing it.

That refusal is important. The earlier wine fantasy was intense, but the poem now wants a subtler intoxication. Poesy, poetry itself, becomes the way to travel without wheels, beasts, or visible wings.

pages.title: Viewless Wings

pages.title: Queen-Moon and Fays
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"Queen-Moon" turns the sky into a court, and the stars into "Fays," or fairies. The night is personified as a kind of enchanted hierarchy, with the moon enthroned and the stars gathered around her.

pages.title: Sight Gives Way

pages.title: The Whole Poem

My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains
My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,
Or emptied some dull opiate to the drains
One minute past, and Lethe-wards had sunk:
'Tis not through envy of thy happy lot,
But being too happy in thine happiness,—
That thou, light-winged Dryad of the trees,
In some melodious plot
Of beechen green, and shadows numberless,
Singest of summer in full-throated ease.

O, for a draught of vintage! that hath been
Cool'd a long age in the deep-delved earth,
Tasting of Flora and the country green,
Dance, and Provençal song, and sunburnt mirth!
O for a beaker full of the warm South,
Full of the true, the blushful Hippocrene,
With beaded bubbles winking at the brim,
And purple-stained mouth;
That I might drink, and leave the world unseen,
And with thee fade away into the forest dim:

Fade far away, dissolve, and quite forget
What thou among the leaves hast never known,
The weariness, the fever, and the fret
Here, where men sit and hear each other groan;
Where palsy shakes a few, sad, last gray hairs,
Where youth grows pale, and spectre-thin, and dies;
Where but to think is to be full of sorrow
And leaden-eyed despairs,
Where Beauty cannot keep her lustrous eyes,
Or new Love pine at them beyond to-morrow.

Away! away! for I will fly to thee,
Not charioted by Bacchus and his pards,
But on the viewless wings of Poesy,
Though the dull brain perplexes and retards:
Already with thee! tender is the night,
And haply the Queen-Moon is on her throne,
Cluster'd around by all her starry Fays;
But here there is no light,
Save what from heaven is with the breezes blown
Through verdurous glooms and winding mossy ways.

I cannot see what flowers are at my feet,
Nor what soft incense hangs upon the boughs,
But, in embalmed darkness, guess each sweet
Wherewith the seasonable month endows
The grass, the thicket, and the fruit-tree wild;
White hawthorn, and the pastoral eglantine;
Fast fading violets cover'd up in leaves;
And mid-May's eldest child,
The coming musk-rose, full of dewy wine,
The murmurous haunt of flies on summer eves.

Darkling I listen; and, for many a time
I have been half in love with easeful Death,
Call'd him soft names in many a mused rhyme,
To take into the air my quiet breath;
Now more than ever seems it rich to die,
To cease upon the midnight with no pain,
While thou art pouring forth thy soul abroad
In such an ecstasy!
Still wouldst thou sing, and I have ears in vain—
To thy high requiem become a sod.

Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!
No hungry generations tread thee down;
The voice I hear this passing night was heard
In ancient days by emperor and clown:
Perhaps the self-same song that found a path
Through the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home,
She stood in tears amid the alien corn;
The same that oft-times hath
Charm'd magic casements, opening on the foam
Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn.

Forlorn! the very word is like a bell
To toll me back from thee to my sole self!
Adieu! the fancy cannot cheat so well
As she is fam'd to do, deceiving elf.
Adieu! adieu! thy plaintive anthem fades
Past the near meadows, over the still stream,
Up the hill-side; and now 'tis buried deep
In the next valley-glades:
Was it a vision, or a waking dream?
Fled is that music:—Do I wake or sleep?

pages.title: Death as Familiar
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The phrase "half in love" is careful. The speaker is not simply suicidal, and the poem should not be flattened into biography. He is describing a recurring imaginative attraction to the idea of painless release.

Still, Keats's life gives the lines weight. He had watched illness at close range, and his own health was fragile. When death appears in this poem, it is not an inherited poetic pose sitting safely on a shelf.

pages.title: Now More Than Ever

pages.title: A Song for the Dead
pages.bodyMarkdown:
A requiem is a mass or musical service for the dead. By calling the nightingale's song a "high requiem," the speaker turns its living ecstasy into funeral music.

The word is double-edged. The bird is not singing mournfully from its own point of view. The speaker hears the song through his deathward imagination, and it changes in his ear.

pages.title: The Cost of Escape

pages.title: What Can Be Immortal
pages.bodyMarkdown:
Keats is not pretending one physical bird has survived from antiquity. The immortality belongs to the bird as type, to the repeated voice of nightingales across time, and to what that voice awakens in human imagination.

This is why the stanza can move so quickly from "this passing night" to "ancient days." One present song opens a corridor backward.

pages.title: Homesick in Alien Corn

pages.title: The Whole Poem
pages.bodyMarkdown:
My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains
My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,
Or emptied some dull opiate to the drains
One minute past, and Lethe-wards had sunk:
'Tis not through envy of thy happy lot,
But being too happy in thine happiness,—
That thou, light-winged Dryad of the trees,
In some melodious plot
Of beechen green, and shadows numberless,
Singest of summer in full-throated ease.

O, for a draught of vintage! that hath been
Cool'd a long age in the deep-delved earth,
Tasting of Flora and the country green,
Dance, and Provençal song, and sunburnt mirth!
O for a beaker full of the warm South,
Full of the true, the blushful Hippocrene,
With beaded bubbles winking at the brim,
And purple-stained mouth;
That I might drink, and leave the world unseen,
And with thee fade away into the forest dim:

Fade far away, dissolve, and quite forget
What thou among the leaves hast never known,
The weariness, the fever, and the fret
Here, where men sit and hear each other groan;
Where palsy shakes a few, sad, last gray hairs,
Where youth grows pale, and spectre-thin, and dies;
Where but to think is to be full of sorrow
And leaden-eyed despairs,
Where Beauty cannot keep her lustrous eyes,
Or new Love pine at them beyond to-morrow.

Away! away! for I will fly to thee,
Not charioted by Bacchus and his pards,
But on the viewless wings of Poesy,
Though the dull brain perplexes and retards:
Already with thee! tender is the night,
And haply the Queen-Moon is on her throne,
Cluster'd around by all her starry Fays;
But here there is no light,
Save what from heaven is with the breezes blown
Through verdurous glooms and winding mossy ways.

I cannot see what flowers are at my feet,
Nor what soft incense hangs upon the boughs,
But, in embalmed darkness, guess each sweet
Wherewith the seasonable month endows
The grass, the thicket, and the fruit-tree wild;
White hawthorn, and the pastoral eglantine;
Fast fading violets cover'd up in leaves;
And mid-May's eldest child,
The coming musk-rose, full of dewy wine,
The murmurous haunt of flies on summer eves.

Darkling I listen; and, for many a time
I have been half in love with easeful Death,
Call'd him soft names in many a mused rhyme,
To take into the air my quiet breath;
Now more than ever seems it rich to die,
To cease upon the midnight with no pain,
While thou art pouring forth thy soul abroad
In such an ecstasy!
Still wouldst thou sing, and I have ears in vain—
To thy high requiem become a sod.

Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!
No hungry generations tread thee down;
The voice I hear this passing night was heard
In ancient days by emperor and clown:
Perhaps the self-same song that found a path
Through the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home,
She stood in tears amid the alien corn;
The same that oft-times hath
Charm'd magic casements, opening on the foam
Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn.

Forlorn! the very word is like a bell
To toll me back from thee to my sole self!
Adieu! the fancy cannot cheat so well
As she is fam'd to do, deceiving elf.
Adieu! adieu! thy plaintive anthem fades
Past the near meadows, over the still stream,
Up the hill-side; and now 'tis buried deep
In the next valley-glades:
Was it a vision, or a waking dream?
Fled is that music:—Do I wake or sleep?

pages.title: The Deceiving Elf
pages.bodyMarkdown:
"Fancy" is imagination in a lighter, more wayward form. Keats personifies her as a "deceiving elf," which sounds playful until you notice how serious the disappointment is.

The speaker wanted poetry to carry him to the bird. Now he admits that imagination cannot cheat reality as well as people say. That is a hard sentence for a poet to write.

pages.title: Near, Over, Up, Next
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The departing song is mapped carefully: near meadows, still stream, hillside, next valley-glades. After faery lands and perilous seas, these are local places again.

That return to ordinary geography matters. The imagination has not erased the world. The speaker is back in a landscape where distance can be tracked and sound can fade.

pages.title: Vision or Waking Dream
pages.bodyMarkdown:
The last two questions are not ornamental. They keep the poem from simplifying itself into a lesson. Was the experience visionary, dreamlike, poetic, sensory, or some mixture of all four?

Keats does not answer. That restraint is part of the poem's intelligence. The speaker has been changed by listening, but he cannot convert that change into certainty.

pages.title: Fled Is That Music

"Do I wake or sleep?" is a question about consciousness, but also about poetry. The poem has made an experience that feels both intensely real and impossible to hold.
